item.description:
Data Structures Lab Notes

Author: 孤筝(lvbowen040427@163.com)

This article merges eight earlier data structures lab reports. The filler and the full source listings are gone; what remains is the core idea, key data structure, and algorithmic essentials of each experiment, as a revision outline. Code snippets are C++.

1. Recursion and the Stack: Fibonacci Numbers

Problem

Compute the $n$-th Fibonacci number recursively.

Why recursion depends on the stack

Whether a recursive call can return correctly depends on two things: how arguments are passed and where to return to. Take Fib(5):

  1. Every recursive level needs fresh storage for that level’s parameters;
  2. The “which line do I resume at when this call finishes” return address must also be saved.

Together these form an activation record, pushed by the system onto the call stack. Calls push, returns pop from the top, and control lands back in the right frame.

For Fib(3) = Fib(2) + Fib(1) the call tree is:

Fib(3)
├── Fib(2)
│   ├── Fib(1) → returns 1
│   └── Fib(0) → returns 0
│   gives 1
└── Fib(1) → returns 1
gives 2

Algorithm 

int Fib(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    if (n == 1) return 1;
    return Fib(n - 1) + Fib(n - 2);
}

This version recomputes the same subproblems over and over, giving exponential time $O(2^n)$. For real use, prefer iteration or memoisation, which is $O(n)$. The recursive form is valuable here because it exposes how the stack works.

2. Partitioning a Set with Conflicts

Problem

Split a set into pairwise disjoint subsets such that no two elements within a subset conflict, using as few subsets as possible. (Typical application: timetabling and scheduling.)

Algorithm: cyclic filtering

  1. Describe the conflicts with a 2-D array (a conflict matrix): $conflict[i][j] = 1$ means $i$ and $j$ conflict, $0$ means they do not.
  2. Take the first ungrouped element and start a new group with it.
  3. Scan the remaining ungrouped elements: if an element conflicts with none of the elements already in the current group, add it; otherwise skip it and leave it for a later round.
  4. When a pass ends with elements still ungrouped, open a new group and repeat from step 2 until everything is grouped.

Data structure

A circular queue holds the pending elements. Each pass rotates them around the queue, so no extra storage is needed.

Key points

  • “Can this element join the group” must be checked against every element already in the group; checking just one gives wrong results.
  • This is a greedy strategy — squeeze in whatever fits now — so it produces a good partition, not necessarily the mathematically optimal one.

3. Sparse Matrix Multiplication

Problem

When a matrix has few non-zero entries, a full 2-D array wastes a lot of space. Store only the non-zeros as triples, then multiply two such matrices.

Data structures 

struct Node {          // one non-zero entry
    int i, j;          // row and column index
    int data;          // value
};

struct Matrix {
    int m, n;          // total rows, total columns
    int L;             // number of non-zero entries
    Node* Ma[MAX];     // array of non-zero entries
};

Algorithm

Following $C_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik} \cdot B_{kj}$, but only accumulating terms where both factors are non-zero:

  1. Walk each non-zero entry $(i, k, a)$ of $A$;
  2. Search $B$ for non-zero entries $(k, j, b)$ whose row index is $k$;
  3. Accumulate $a \times b$ into position $(i, j)$ of the result.

Result entries are created on demand; if an accumulation ends at 0, nothing is stored.

Key points

  • Far faster than the naive triple loop, because multiplications by zero are skipped entirely.
  • To speed it up further, add a row index to the triple list (a row-linked list) so step 2 does not rescan $B$ from scratch each time.
  • Validate that the number of columns of $A$ equals the number of rows of $B$, and that input indices are in range.

4. KMP String Matching

Problem

Find the first occurrence of a pattern in a text. Naive matching shifts the pattern right by one and rewinds the text pointer on a mismatch, which is $O(nm)$ in the worst case. KMP brings it down to $O(n+m)$.

The core: the LPS array

LPS (longest prefix suffix) records, for each position of the pattern, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of the substring before that position. It tells us how far the pattern may safely slide on a mismatch, so the text pointer never has to move backwards.

For the pattern ABABCABAB:

Index 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
Char A B A B C A B A B
LPS 0 0 1 2 0 1 2 3 4

Algorithm 

// build the LPS array
void computeLPS(const string& pat, vector<int>& lps) {
    int len = 0;          // current longest prefix-suffix match
    lps[0] = 0;
    int i = 1;
    while (i < (int)pat.size()) {
        if (pat[i] == pat[len]) {
            lps[i++] = ++len;
        } else if (len != 0) {
            len = lps[len - 1];   // fall back to the next-longest border
        } else {
            lps[i++] = 0;
        }
    }
}

// search for pat inside text
void KMPSearch(const string& text, const string& pat) {
    int m = pat.size(), n = text.size();
    vector<int> lps(m);
    computeLPS(pat, lps);

    int i = 0, j = 0;          // i walks the text, j walks the pattern
    while (i < n) {
        if (pat[j] == text[i]) { i++; j++; }
        if (j == m) {
            cout << "Match found at index " << i - j << endl;
            j = lps[j - 1];    // keep searching for further matches
        } else if (i < n && pat[j] != text[i]) {
            if (j != 0) j = lps[j - 1];
            else        i++;   // j is already 0, so advance the text pointer instead
        }
    }
}

Key points

  • The text pointer i never moves backwards — that is where KMP’s efficiency comes from.
  • On a mismatch, fall back with lps[j-1] rather than resetting j to zero.
  • The lps construction is itself “matching the pattern against itself” and mirrors the main loop.
  • Example: text ABABDABACDABABCABAB, pattern ABABCABAB — the match starts at index 10.

5. Binary Trees: Storage and Traversal

Problem

Given a string of characters in level order (BFS order) where @ marks a missing node, build a binary tree, then implement traversal for both array-based and pointer-based storage.

Two storage schemes

Sequential (array) storage: parent/child relations are computed from indices:

  • Parent at index $i$ → left child $2i+1$, right child $2i+2$;
  • Conversely, the parent of node $i$ is $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$.

Suits complete binary trees; with a sparse tree most of the array is wasted.

Linked storage: a struct with pointers, built with the help of a queue.

struct TreeNode {
    char data;
    TreeNode* left;
    TreeNode* right;
};

Construction: push the root, then repeatedly pop a node from the front and attach its left and right children in turn (an @ means that side stays empty), pushing each new child. To build from preorder input instead, swap the queue for a stack.

The three depth-first traversals 

void preOrder(TreeNode* p) {          // root → left → right
    if (!p) return;
    visit(p);
    preOrder(p->left);
    preOrder(p->right);
}

void inOrder(TreeNode* p) {           // left → root → right
    if (!p) return;
    inOrder(p->left);
    visit(p);
    inOrder(p->right);
}

void postOrder(TreeNode* p) {         // left → right → root
    if (!p) return;
    postOrder(p->left);
    postOrder(p->right);
    visit(p);
}

Breadth-first traversal

Use a queue to process the tree level by level: on visiting a node, push its left then right child.

void levelOrder(TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return;
    queue<TreeNode*> q;
    q.push(root);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        TreeNode* p = q.front(); q.pop();
        visit(p);
        if (p->left)  q.push(p->left);
        if (p->right) q.push(p->right);
    }
}

Worked example

Input abc@def@@@@ (level order, @ empty) describes this tree:

        a
      /   \
     b     c
    / \   / \
   @   d e   f
      / \ / \ / \
     @  @ @ @ @  @
Traversal Result
preorder (root, left, right) a b d c e f
inorder (left, root, right) b d a e c f
postorder (left, right, root) d b e f c a
level order (BFS) a b c d e f

With array storage, take care where an inorder walk starts: preorder may start at index 0, but inorder must start at the leftmost node of the whole tree, or the left half of the left subtree is missed.

Reconstructing a tree from traversals

  • preorder + inorder, postorder + inorder, and level order + inorder each determine a unique binary tree.
  • preorder + postorder does not, because it cannot tell whether a lone child hangs on the left or the right.

6. Huffman Trees and Coding

Problem

Assign codes to characters according to their frequency so that the encoded text is as short as possible and no code is a prefix of another (a prefix code, which guarantees unique decoding).

Algorithm

  1. Count the frequency of every character.
  2. Create one leaf node per character and push them all into a min-heap.
  3. While more than one node remains: pop the two least frequent nodes, merge them into a new internal node whose frequency is their sum, and push it back.
  4. When one node is left, it is the root of the Huffman tree.
while (minHeap.size() > 1) {
    auto left  = minHeap.top(); minHeap.pop();
    auto right = minHeap.top(); minHeap.pop();
    auto parent = new HuffmanNode('$', left->frequency + right->frequency);
    parent->left = left;
    parent->right = right;
    minHeap.push(parent);
}

Encoding and decoding

  • Generate codes: recurse from the root, appending 0 when going left and 1 when going right; at a leaf, the accumulated string is that character’s code.
  • Encode: replace every character of the input with its code.
  • Decode: start at the root, follow 0 left and 1 right, and on reaching a leaf emit that character and restart from the root.

Key points

  • Frequent characters sit close to the root and get short codes — that is the whole idea behind compression.
  • Because every character lives at a leaf, no code can be a prefix of another, so decoding is unambiguous.
  • Using a min-heap instead of repeated sorting brings construction down to $O(n \log n)$.
  • Characters with equal frequency may be ordered either way without changing any code length; only which bit string each receives changes.

7. Binary Search Trees and Deletion

Problem

Build a binary search tree (BST) supporting insertion, inorder traversal, and node deletion.

Insertion

Compare recursively: smaller goes left, larger goes right, and an empty slot gets a new node.

TreeNode* insert(TreeNode* root, int val) {
    if (!root) return new TreeNode(val);
    if (val < root->val)      root->left  = insert(root->left,  val);
    else if (val > root->val) root->right = insert(root->right, val);
    return root;   // duplicates are not inserted
}

Inorder traversal

An inorder walk of a BST yields an increasing sequence — the quickest sanity check that the tree was built correctly.

Deleting a node

Deletion is the easiest step to get wrong. There are three cases:

Case Handling
Leaf (no children) delete it directly
Exactly one child let that child take its place
Two children replace its value with the smallest node in the right subtree (the inorder successor), then recursively delete that successor 
TreeNode* remove(TreeNode* root, int val) {
    if (!root) return nullptr;
    if (val < root->val)      root->left  = remove(root->left,  val);
    else if (val > root->val) root->right = remove(root->right, val);
    else {
        if (!root->left)  { auto t = root->right; delete root; return t; }
        if (!root->right) { auto t = root->left;  delete root; return t; }
        // two children: find the smallest node of the right subtree
        TreeNode* succ = root->right;
        while (succ->left) succ = succ->left;
        root->val   = succ->val;
        root->right = remove(root->right, succ->val);
    }
    return root;
}

Replacing with the largest node of the left subtree (the inorder predecessor) is equally valid.

Deleting the whole tree

Free nodes in postorder; releasing a parent before its children loses the pointers you still need.

8. Threaded Binary Trees

Problem

A binary tree with $n$ nodes has $2n$ pointer fields, but only $n-1$ edges are actually used, leaving $n+1$ null pointers wasted. Threading reuses those nulls to store the predecessor/successor under some traversal order, so traversal no longer needs a stack or recursion.

Data structure 

struct Node {
    int data;
    Node *left, *right;
    int ltag, rtag;   // 0: points to a child; 1: it is a thread (predecessor/successor)
};

Algorithm (inorder threading)

Walk the tree inorder recursively while keeping a global pre pointer to the last visited node:

Node* pre = nullptr;

void thread(Node* p) {
    if (!p) return;
    thread(p->left);              // handle the left subtree first

    if (!p->left) {               // left child empty: point it at the predecessor
        p->left = pre;
        p->ltag = 1;
    }
    if (pre && !pre->right) {     // predecessor's right child empty: point it here
        pre->right = p;
        pre->rtag = 1;
    }

    pre = p;                      // advance the predecessor
    thread(p->right);             // then the right subtree
}

Key points

  • left / right are overloaded: only ltag / rtag distinguish a child from a thread. Mistaking a thread for a child pointer leads to infinite loops.
  • Inorder threading must recurse left first, then handle the current node, then recurse right; where pre = p sits determines what the threads point at.
  • Preorder and postorder threading follow the same idea; what changes is when the current node is processed and the order of pre updates.
  • A threaded tree traverses in $O(1)$ extra space, with no stack and no recursion.

9. Graph Storage: Adjacency Matrix vs. Adjacency List

Adjacency matrix

Store edges in a 2-D array adj[V][V]: adj[i][j] = 1 (or the edge weight) means an edge $i \to j$ exists.

  • Pros: testing whether two vertices are adjacent is $O(1)$; simple to implement.
  • Cons: space is always $O(V^2)$, which is very wasteful for sparse graphs; enumerating a vertex’s neighbours scans a whole row, $O(V)$.
  • For an undirected graph the matrix is symmetric about the main diagonal.

Adjacency list

An array of lists: adj[i] holds every vertex adjacent to $i$.

vector<int> adj[MAX];          // each element is a linked list / dynamic array
void addEdge(int u, int v) {
    adj[u].push_back(v);
    adj[v].push_back(u);       // add the reverse edge for undirected graphs
}
  • Pros: space $O(V + E)$, friendly to sparse graphs; enumerating neighbours touches only edges that exist.
  • Cons: testing adjacency requires scanning a list, $O(V)$ worst case.
  • In a directed graph, adj[u] holds outgoing edges, so computing in-degrees needs an extra pass or a separate reverse adjacency list.

Choosing between them

Situation Choice
Dense graph, frequent adjacency queries adjacency matrix
Sparse graph, frequent neighbour enumeration adjacency list
Very many vertices (say $10^5$) adjacency list (a matrix will not fit)

Checks when building a graph

After reading an edge $(u, v)$, validate $0 \le u, v < V$ to avoid out-of-range access; for unweighted graphs, do not add the same edge twice, as it distorts traversals and degree counts.

10. Kruskal and Minimum Spanning Trees

Problem

Find a spanning tree of minimum total weight in a weighted connected undirected graph.

Algorithm (greedy)

  1. Sort all edges by weight ascending.
  2. Consider each edge in turn: if its endpoints are not yet in the same set, add the edge to the tree and merge the two sets; otherwise adding it would create a cycle, so discard it.
  3. Stop once $V-1$ edges have been chosen.
sort(edges.begin(), edges.end(),
     [](const Edge& a, const Edge& b) { return a.weight < b.weight; });

UnionFind uf(numNodes);
vector<Edge> result;
for (const Edge& e : edges) {
    if (uf.find(e.start) != uf.find(e.end)) {   // disconnected → safe to add
        result.push_back(e);
        uf.unite(e.start, e.end);
    }
}

Union-Find

Kruskal hinges on “are these two vertices already connected?”, which is exactly what a disjoint-set structure answers well:

  • Find(x): locate the root of $x$’s set, which also tells whether two vertices share a set.
  • Union(a, b): merge two sets.

Two optimisations together make the amortised cost nearly constant:

Optimisation Technique Effect
Path compression on Find, hang every visited node directly off the root sharply reduces tree height
Union by rank attach the shorter tree under the taller one prevents lopsided trees 
int find(int x) {
    if (parent[x] != x) parent[x] = find(parent[x]);   // path compression
    return parent[x];
}

void unite(int a, int b) {
    a = find(a); b = find(b);
    if (a == b) return;
    if (rank[a] < rank[b]) swap(a, b);   // union by rank
    parent[b] = a;
    if (rank[a] == rank[b]) rank[a]++;
}

Key points

  • Time complexity is $O(E \log E)$, dominated by the sort.
  • Best suited to sparse graphs. For dense graphs Prim’s algorithm ($O(V^2)$, or $O(E \log V)$ with a heap) is usually faster.
  • Sorting the edges and using Union-Find for cycle detection are the two moves at the heart of Kruskal.

11. Dijkstra and Single-Source Shortest Paths

Problem

Given a weighted graph and a source $s$, find the shortest distance from $s$ to every other vertex.

Algorithm (greedy + priority queue)

  1. Set the source distance to 0 and all others to infinity.
  2. Put (distance, vertex) pairs into a priority queue and repeatedly extract the vertex $u$ with the smallest distance — its shortest distance is now final.
  3. Relax: for each neighbour $v$ of $u$, if $dist[u] + w(u,v) < dist[v]$ then update $dist[v]$ and push the new (dist[v], v) pair.
  4. Repeat 2–3 until the queue is empty.
vector<int> dijkstra(const vector<vector<int>>& g, int src) {
    int n = g.size();
    vector<int> dist(n, INF);
    // min-heap: the smallest element always sits at the front
    priority_queue<pair<int,int>, vector<pair<int,int>>, greater<>> pq;

    dist[src] = 0;
    pq.push({0, src});

    while (!pq.empty()) {
        auto [d, u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;        // stale entry, skip it
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) {
            if (g[u][v] == 0) continue;   // 0 means no direct edge
            if (dist[u] + g[u][v] < dist[v]) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + g[u][v];
                pq.push({dist[v], v});
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

Key points

  • Negative edge weights are not supported. Dijkstra’s correctness relies on an extracted vertex’s distance never decreasing again, and negative edges break that assumption; use Bellman-Ford or SPFA instead.
  • With an adjacency matrix the inner scan is $O(V)$ and the total is $O(V^2)$; switching to an adjacency list with a priority queue brings it to $O(E \log V)$.
  • A vertex may be pushed several times, so skip stale entries by checking d > dist[u] on pop.
  • Using 0 to mean “no edge” is a convention; if zero-weight edges are legitimate, use a separate marker or an adjacency list.

12. Critical Paths

Problem

In an AON (activity-on-node) network, where each vertex is an activity with a duration and precedence constraints, find the sequence of activities that determines the project’s total duration.

  • Earliest start (ES): the soonest an activity can begin.
  • Latest start (LS): the latest it may begin without delaying the whole project.
  • Slack: $LS - ES$. Activities with zero slack are the critical activities, and together they form the critical path.

Forward pass for ES

Process the topological order from the start events towards the end:

$$ES[v] = \max_{u \in pred(v)} \big( ES[u] + duration[u] \big)$$

An initial activity with no predecessors gets $ES = 0$. The project duration is $T = \max_v (ES[v] + duration[v])$.

void calcEarliest() {
    // must process in topological order, or a predecessor's ES is not ready yet
    for (int u : topoOrder) {
        for (int v : activities[u].next) {
            earliest[v] = max(earliest[v], earliest[u] + activities[u].duration);
        }
    }
}

Backward pass for LS

Walk the reverse topological order back from the end events:

$$LS[u] = \min_{v \in succ(u)} \big( LS[v] \big) - duration[u]$$

A terminal activity with no successors has $LS = ES = T - duration$. (Equivalently, set $LF[\cdot] = T$, so $LS = LF - duration$ and $LF[u] = \min_{v \in succ(u)} LS[v]$.)

void calcLatest() {
    for (int u : reverseTopoOrder) {
        for (int v : activities[u].next) {
            latest[u] = min(latest[u], latest[v] - activities[u].duration);
        }
    }
}

Key points

  • Both passes must proceed strictly in topological order, or the predecessors/successors being read have not been computed yet.
  • Do not identify start events by “the adjacency list is empty” — an empty adjacency list marks an end event (out-degree 0). Start events are those with in-degree 0; getting this backwards invalidates the whole computation.
  • There may be more than one critical path; mark every activity whose slack is 0.
  • To shorten the project you can only compress critical activities; compressing the others achieves nothing.

Summary

Experiment Core data structure Key point
Fibonacci call stack recursion relies on the stack for parameters and return addresses
Set partitioning conflict matrix + circular queue compare against all group members; greedy grouping
Sparse matrix multiply triple list accumulate only terms non-zero on both sides
KMP LPS array the text pointer never moves backwards
Binary trees array / linked nodes index-based parent/child relations; three DFS orders plus BFS
Huffman min-heap repeatedly merge the two least frequent nodes
BST linked nodes deletion has three cases; inorder gives a sorted sequence
Threading nodes with tag bits ltag/rtag distinguish children from threads
Graph storage adjacency matrix / list dense → matrix, sparse → list
Kruskal edge list + Union-Find sort edges, detect cycles with Union-Find
Dijkstra priority queue greedy relaxation; no negative weights
Critical path DAG + topological order forward for ES, backward for LS; zero slack is critical

item.description:
MicroPython Function Reference

Author: 孤筝(lvbowen040427@163.com)

This article collects the parts of MicroPython’s machine module that are most useful on a Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040). Everything has been checked against the official MicroPython documentation.

machine: Hardware-Related Functions

There are two numbering schemes for pins:

  • GPIO number (GP0–GP29): the one used in code; Pin(25) means GP25.
  • Physical pin number: the 40 header positions on the board. These are not the same as GPIO numbers, so be careful when wiring.

class Pin

Constructor machine.Pin(id, mode=-1, pull=-1, value=None)

Parameter Meaning
id Pin identifier. On the Pico, 0–29 (GP0–GP29)
mode None / Pin.IN(0) / Pin.OUT(1) / Pin.OPEN_DRAIN(2)
pull Internal pull resistor, valid only in input mode: None / Pin.PULL_UP(1) / Pin.PULL_DOWN(2)
value Valid only for output/open-drain mode; initial level: 0 low, 1 high

Note that it is Pin.PULL_DOWN, not Pin.DOWN.

Pin.init(mode=-1, pull=-1, value=None)

Re-initialise the pin. Only the arguments you pass are changed; everything else keeps its current state.

Pin.value([x])

  • With no argument: returns the current pin level (0 or 1).
  • With an argument: writes the level. The argument is converted to a boolean (True sets 1, False sets 0).

Pin.on() / Pin.off() and Pin.high() / Pin.low()

  • on(), high(): drive the pin high (1).
  • off(), low(): drive the pin low (0).

These four are meaningful only in output/open-drain mode. low() and high() are not part of the core API, but they are available on the Pico (rp2 port).

Pin.toggle()

Flips the output level from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0. toggle() is available on the rp2, esp32, and several other ports; where it is missing, use Pin.value(not Pin.value()) instead.

from machine import Pin
import time

led = Pin(25, Pin.OUT)   # the on-board LED of a Pico is GP25
while True:
    led.toggle()
    time.sleep(1)        # flip once per second

Pin.irq(handler=None, trigger=Pin.IRQ_FALLING | Pin.IRQ_RISING)

Configures an external interrupt. The callback runs whenever the trigger condition occurs.

  • handler: the callback, which must accept one Pin argument.
  • trigger: the condition, and multiple values can be OR-ed with |:
Constant Trigger
Pin.IRQ_FALLING falling edge
Pin.IRQ_RISING rising edge
Pin.IRQ_LOW_LEVEL low level
Pin.IRQ_HIGH_LEVEL high level 
def on_press(pin):
    print("Button pressed")

button = Pin(15, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
button.irq(handler=on_press, trigger=Pin.IRQ_FALLING)

class PWM

PWM (pulse-width modulation) switches a pin on and off rapidly to emulate intermediate voltages. It is used for dimming LEDs, controlling motor speed, and driving servos.

machine.PWM(pin, freq=..., duty_u16=...)

Creates a PWM output on the given pin; pin is a Pin object.

Common methods

Method Purpose
PWM.freq([value]) get/set the frequency in Hz, roughly 8 Hz – 62.5 MHz (at a 125 MHz CPU clock)
PWM.duty_u16([value]) get/set the duty cycle as 0–65535, the ratio value / 65535
PWM.duty_ns([value]) get/set the high time within one period, in nanoseconds
PWM.deinit() stop the PWM output

The upper bound of duty_u16 is 65535, not 65536. Passing 65536 overflows.

RP2040 has 8 independent PWM slices with 2 channels each, 16 channels in total. The two channels of a slice must share a frequency but may have different duty cycles.

Example: breathing LED 

from machine import Pin, PWM
import time

led = PWM(Pin(25))
led.freq(1000)      # 1 kHz

duty = 0            # duty cycle in percent
step = 1

while True:
    duty += step
    if duty >= 100:
        duty = 100
        step = -1
    elif duty <= 0:
        duty = 0
        step = 1

    # convert percent to the 0-65535 range, without overflowing
    led.duty_u16(int(duty / 100 * 65535))

    if duty % 5 == 0:
        print(duty)  # convenient for plotting

    time.sleep(0.01)  # roughly a 2-second round trip

Example: button-controlled LED (with software debouncing) 

from machine import Pin
import time

button = Pin(15, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)   # reads 0 while pressed
led_board = Pin(25, Pin.OUT)            # on-board LED
led_ext = Pin(16, Pin.OUT)              # external LED

while True:
    led_ext.off()
    if button.value() == 0:             # possibly pressed
        time.sleep(0.01)                # wait 10 ms and check again to filter bounce
        if button.value() == 0:         # confirmed
            led_board.toggle()
            led_ext.on()
            print("The button is pressed.")
            while button.value() == 0:  # wait for release
                time.sleep(0.01)

A mechanical button bounces for a few milliseconds when pressed or released, and the CPU can read that as several presses. Software debouncing means: after detecting a change, wait about 10 ms and read the pin again to confirm.

class ADC

The ADC (analog-to-digital converter) turns an analog voltage into a digital reading.

machine.ADC(id)

id may be a Pin object or a channel number:

  • On the Pico, channels 0–3 map to GP26–GP29 (GP29 is wired to VSYS on the board);
  • Channel 4 is the on-chip temperature sensor, also reachable as ADC.CORE_TEMP.

ADC.read_u16()

Returns the reading as an integer in 0–65535, spanning the input range 0–3.3 V.

from machine import ADC, Pin

adc = ADC(Pin(26))          # equivalent to ADC(0)
value = adc.read_u16()      # 0 - 65535
voltage = value / 65535 * 3.3   # convert to volts
print(voltage, "V")

The range is 0–65535. The RP2040’s ADC hardware is only 12-bit (0–4095); MicroPython scales it linearly to 16 bits, so the lowest few bits carry no real precision.

Summary

Task Key point
Digital I/O Pin(id, mode, pull); read with value(), write with value() / on() / off() / toggle()
Interrupts Pin.irq(handler, trigger); the callback must take one Pin argument
Dimming / speed control PWM(pin) + freq() + duty_u16(); duty is capped at 65535
Reading analog input ADC(Pin(26)) + read_u16(), returning 0–65535
Button bounce after detecting a change, wait 10 ms and confirm

Python Basics

Author: 孤筝(lvbowen040427@163.com)

This article merges four earlier Python notes, removes duplicated and irrelevant material, and keeps only what is useful as a day-to-day reference. Examples target Python 3.

Variables and Objects

  • Variables need no type declaration, but they must be assigned before use, otherwise a NameError is raised.
  • Python has no const and no mechanism preventing reassignment; a “constant” is only a naming convention (all caps).
  • = assigns; == compares.
>>> age
NameError: name 'age' is not defined

A useful mental model: objects are the data, variables are labels stuck onto objects.

a = "Jack"   # create the string object "Jack", then stick the label a onto it
b = a        # stick label b onto the same object; this is not a copy
id(a) == id(b)   # True, both refer to the same object
a = "Ross"   # a different object gets the label a; b still refers to "Jack"
  • An object can carry many labels, but a variable refers to exactly one object at a time.
  • The variable itself has no type; the type belongs to the object. So a = 1 followed by a = "1" is perfectly legal.

Assignment and Slicing

= is right-associative, so a = b = c = 1 makes all three names refer to the integer object 1.

a, b, c = 1, 2, 3   # unpacking assignment
age = 17 + 1        # evaluate the right side first

Slicing works on strings, tuples, and lists with the syntax obj[a:b:c]:

Form Meaning
obj[a:b] Indices in $[a, b)$, excluding b; omit a to start at 0, omit b to run to the end
obj[a:b:c] Take every c-th element; c defaults to 1
negative c Walk backwards
obj[::-1] Reverse (returns a new object; the original is unchanged) 
>>> name = "polaris"
>>> name[1:3]
'ol'
>>> name[::-3]
'sap'
>>> name[::-1]
'siralop'

Slicing also copies: y = x[:] gives a shallow copy, so sorting y does not affect x.

Strings

  1. Single and double quotes are equivalent; there is no separate single-character type.
  2. Triple quotes allow multi-line strings.
  3. To include the same quote character inside a string, escape it: \".

Three ways to format 

name, age = "Bronya", 18

print('My wife is %s, she is %d.' % (name, age))          # % formatting, the oldest
print('My wife is {}, she is {}.'.format(name, age))      # .format()
print(f'My wife is {name}, she is {age}.')                # f-string, recommended
  • % formatting takes a tuple or dict and substitutes positionally or by name.
  • In .format(), {} may use positional indices {0} or keywords {name}.
  • f-strings require Python 3.6+ and are the most readable; all three support width, alignment, and precision specifiers.

Numbers and Booleans

Type Notes
int Arbitrary-precision integer; supports 0x hex, 0o octal, 0b binary literals
float Floating point; scientific notation such as 1.23e-6
complex Complex numbers, written a + bj or complex(a, b)
bool True is really 1 and False is really 0
NoneType The null value; None must be capitalised
  • Mixing an int with a float promotes the int: 1 + 2.0 gives 3.0.
  • Floats carry rounding error: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False (the actual value is 0.30000000000000004). Use the decimal module when exact arithmetic is required.
  • round() uses banker’s rounding (round-half-to-even): round(0.5) is 0, round(1.5) is 2, round(2.5) is 2.

Falsy values: 0, 0.0, None, empty string, empty list, empty tuple, empty dict, empty set, False. Everything else is truthy, including any non-empty string (even the string "False").

Operators

Arithmetic

Operator Meaning Example
+ - * addition, subtraction, multiplication
/ true division; the result is always a float 6 / 3 → 2.0
// floor division, rounds down 7 // 2 → 3, -7 // 2 → -4
% modulo (remainder) 7 % 2 → 1
** power, right-associative 2 ** 2 ** 3 → 256
- unary minus, binds weaker than ** -2 ** 2 → -4

The rest

Category Operators
Comparison == != < <= > >=; can be chained: a > b == c means a > b and b == c
Logical and or not
Membership in not in
Identity is is not; compares whether two names refer to the same object (compares id, not value)
Bitwise & | ^ ~ << >>
Augmented assignment += -= *= //= **= &= |= ^= <<= >>=

and / or return one of their operands, not True / False:

>>> True and 0 + 3
3
>>> False or 31
31
>>> 0 or 0
0

Precedence (highest to lowest)

() → indexing [] → attribute . → ** → unary ~ + - → * / % // → + - → << >> → & → ^ → | → comparisons (<, ==, in, is, all one level) → not → and → or → assignment

If you cannot remember it, just add parentheses; that is the cheapest fix.

Input, Output, and Built-in Functions 

print(self, *args, sep=' ', end='\n', file=None)   # sep between items, end after the last
age = input("Enter your age: ")   # the return value is always a string
int(age)                          # convert explicitly when you need a number

Common built-ins:

Function Purpose
id(x) memory address (identity) of the object
type(x) the object’s type, e.g. <class 'int'>
len(x) number of elements
abs() round() bool() absolute value, rounding, boolean conversion
enumerate(seq, start=0) index and value together while looping
range() zip() sum() max() min() sorted() common sequence helpers

Type-conversion functions: int(x, base), float(), complex(), str(), repr(), chr(), ord(), hex(), oct(), eval(), list(), tuple(), set(), frozenset(), dict().

Conversion is not unconditional; it depends on whether the source data carries enough information to express the target type. int("123") works, int("Hello") raises an error; a list can become a set, but not a single number.

Implicit conversion follows a precision order: bool < int < float < complex, moving toward the more precise type in mixed expressions.

galgames = ['Cafe', 'Senren Banka', 'Tenshi Sou Sou']
for index, galgame in enumerate(galgames, 1):
    print(f'Playing game number {index}: {galgame}')

Conditionals and Loops 

if condition1:
    ...
elif condition2:
    ...
else:
    ...

for iterates over anything iterable (lists, dicts, strings, tuples, generators, …):

for x in sequence:
    ...

for i in range(5):
    ...
  • break leaves only the innermost loop.
  • continue skips the rest of this iteration and goes to the next.
  • for ... else / while ... else: the else runs when the loop completes normally; it is skipped if the loop was left via break.
while condition:
    ...

When writing a while, always confirm that the body eventually changes the condition or triggers a break; otherwise you have an infinite loop.

The Four Container Types

Container Literal Ordered Mutable Duplicates Element requirement
list [1, 2] yes yes yes any
tuple (1, 2) yes no yes any
dict {k: v} insertion order yes keys unique keys must be hashable
set {1, 2} no yes no (auto-deduplicated) must be hashable

list 

a = []                  # empty list
a.append(x)             # append to the end
a.insert(i, x)          # insert at index i, shifting later elements right
a.extend(b)             # append each element of b
a.pop()                 # remove and return the last element
a.pop(i)                # remove and return the element at index i
a.remove(x)             # remove the first element equal to x; errors if absent
a.index(x)              # index of the first element equal to x
a.count(x)              # how many elements equal x
a.reverse()             # reverse in place
a.sort(key=..., reverse=False)   # sort in place; returns None
del a[i]                # delete the element at index i
del a[1:3]              # delete a slice

Sorting example:

random = [(2, 2), (3, 4), (4, 1), (1, 3)]
random.sort(key=lambda e: e[1])   # sort by the second element of each tuple
# [(4, 1), (2, 2), (1, 3), (3, 4)]

Note: sort() accepts only key and reverse. The Python 2 cmp parameter was removed.

tuple

  • Tuples are immutable: no insert, update, or delete.
  • A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (1,) is a tuple, (1) is just the integer.
  • Conversion: list(t) yields a list, tuple(l) yields a tuple. The original object is unchanged; a new object is returned.

dict 

profile = {'name': 'Guzheng', 'age': 19}
profile2 = dict(name='Guzheng', age=19)              # with = the keys are unquoted
profile3 = dict([('name', 'Guzheng'), ('age', 19)])  # built from key-value pairs
profile4 = {i: i ** 2 for i in range(2, 5)}          # {2: 4, 3: 9, 4: 16}

Access and update:

profile['name']                 # raises KeyError if the key is absent
profile.get('gender')           # returns None if absent
profile.get('gender', 'male')   # returns a default if absent
profile.setdefault('gender', 'male')   # writes the pair if absent, then returns it
profile['gender'] = 'male'      # add or update
del profile['age']
profile.pop('age')

The key distinction: get() is read-only and never modifies the dict; only setdefault() writes when the key is missing.

Test for a key with in / not in. has_key() is the Python 2 spelling and was removed in Python 3.

set 

s = {1, 2, 2, 3}     # deduplicated automatically to {1, 2, 3}
s = set()            # the only way to write an empty set; {} is an empty dict
Operation Method Operator
union a.union(b) a | b
intersection a.intersection(b) a & b
difference (in a, not in b) a.difference(b) a - b
symmetric difference a.symmetric_difference(b) a ^ b
  • Add: add(x) (only hashable/immutable values), update(seq) (accepts a string, list, tuple, or set; given a dict it takes only the keys).
  • Remove: remove(x) errors if absent; discard(x) does not; pop() removes and returns an arbitrary element and takes no argument; clear() empties the set.
  • Test: x in s, a.isdisjoint(b) (True when they share nothing), b.issubset(a).
  • Sets are unordered and unindexed: you cannot read or modify elements by position, only add and remove.

Common misconception: pop() removes an arbitrary element, not a random one. Storage order follows hash values, so it looks random but is not under your control.

Iterators and Generators

Iterable: anything you can loop over with for. It qualifies if either holds:

  1. it implements __iter__() returning an iterator instance;
  2. it has no __iter__() but implements __getitem__() and supports indexing from 0 upward.

Iterator: what iter(iterable) returns. Call next() repeatedly to pull values; when exhausted it raises StopIteration.

from collections.abc import Iterable, Iterator

isinstance([], Iterable)        # True, a list is iterable
isinstance([], Iterator)        # False, but a list is not itself an iterator
isinstance(iter([]), Iterator)  # True

In other words, a list is iterable but not an iterator: a list can be traversed repeatedly, while an iterator moves forward only once.

A generator is “an iterator written as a function”:

# list comprehension produces a list
alist = [i for i in range(5)]     # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

# parentheses produce a generator
agen = (i for i in range(5))      # <generator object ...>, lazily evaluated

Note: (i for i in ...) is a generator expression, not a tuple comprehension. Python has no tuple comprehension. To get a tuple, write tuple(i for i in ...).

yield versus return: when execution reaches yield, the function pauses and hands out a value without ending; the next request resumes right after the pause, until the function finishes. A bare yield produces None.

def generator():
    i = 0
    while i < 5:
        i += 1
        yield i

gen = generator()
next(gen)   # 1

for v in generator():
    print(v)   # 1 2 3 4 5

The value of a generator is laziness: it never computes every result at once, so it uses far less memory than a list when handling large data streams.

Other Notes

Comments 

# a single-line comment

'''
Triple quotes are technically a "multi-line string", not a comment:
the interpreter really does create a string object, it is simply an unused expression.
'''

Because it is a string rather than a comment, dropping triple quotes into the middle of code breaks the syntax and often raises an error. The correct habit is to use # for comments.

Source encoding

  • Python 3 source files are UTF-8 by default, so you normally do not need an encoding declaration.
  • Only Python 2 required a header line, which is now essentially obsolete:
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

Identifiers

  • Composed of letters, digits, and underscores, cannot start with a digit, and are case-sensitive.
  • Python 3 permits non-ASCII (including Chinese) names, but this is discouraged.
  • Underscore conventions:
    • _name: single leading underscore, meaning “internal use”; from module import * will not import it.
    • __age: double leading underscore, triggering name mangling to avoid clashes in subclasses.
    • __init__: leading and trailing double underscores mark a built-in special method; do not invent such names yourself.
